references.text: In Jesus' parable of the two sons in [ref:Matt 21:28-31|Matthew 21:28-31], the motif "a man had two sons" (Ἄνθρωπος εἶχεν τέκνα δύο) is also used as a starting point for a parable about obedience and repentance, which thematically is closely related to the parable of the lost son.

The context for the parable: [ref:Luk 15:1-2|Luke 15:1-2] tells us that tax collectors and sinners came to hear Jesus, while the Pharisees and scribes grumbled about it. The parable of the lost son is Jesus' response to this criticism, and the two sons represent exactly these two groups.

The parable of the lost son is the third in a series of three parables about what was lost in [ref:Luk 15:4-7|Luke 15:4-7] (the lost sheep). All three parables deal with God's joy over finding what was lost.
The second parable in the series about what was lost, [ref:Luk 15:8-10|Luke 15:8-10] (the lost coin), shares the same theme of God's grace and joy over the one who repents.

The motif of two sons (or brothers) representing different life paths is already found in [ref:1 Mos 25:23-34|Genesis 25:23-34], the story of Esau and Jacob. The younger son who leaves and then returns reminds us of Jacob's story.

[ref:Ordsp 29:3|Proverbs 29:3]: "He who loves wisdom rejoices his father, but he who keeps company with prostitutes squanders his wealth." This summarizes the fate of the younger son in the parable, where he wastes his inheritance on a dissolute life.
